title: Young spanish adults and disinformation: Do they identify and spread fake news and are they literate in it?
screen_reason: Nationally quota-matched online survey of 501 Spanish adults aged 18-25 (Netquest panel, 23 July - 14 August 2020). Section 3.3 and Table 14 report two self-reported shares with an explicit denominator: 87.6% have at some time received fake news (RECALL-exposure) and 6.6% have knowingly spread a fake news item (RECALL-sharing). Both are shares of respondents reporting any lifetime occurrence, which the protocol counts as RECALL.

estimates.platform: Any medium (survey question wording: 'through any medium'; the questionnaire elsewhere names the Internet, WhatsApp, Instagram, TikTok and email)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who say they have ever received fake news through any medium
estimates.value_raw: Have received fake news 87.6% (Table 14, Total n = 501)
estimates.denominator: 501 Spanish adults aged 18-25 interviewed online (Netquest panel, quota-matched to the National Institute of Statistics distribution of sex, age, region and social class; sampling error +/-4.47%, 95% confidence)
estimates.definition: Respondent answered yes to Q9: 'Have you ever received, through any medium, fake news?' Fake news was introduced to respondents as 'fake news, a rumor, a hoax, a lie'.
estimates.misinfo_def: "The Ethical Journalism Network (EJN) defines fake news as 'information deliberately fabricated and published with the intention to deceive and mislead others into believing falsehoods or doubting verifiable facts'"
estimates.source_quote: We found 87.6% of young people have at some time received fake news, especially women (91.5%), those with the highest level of education (93.7%) and social class (90.7%), while 6.6% claim to have spread fake news at some point, compared to 93.5% who do not tend to spread such news (Table 14).
estimates.page_loc: Section 3.3 Dissemination of Fake News, p. 11; Table 14, p. 12
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Pure respondent self-report; no external verification of any item. Single dichotomous questionnaire item (Q9) in a structured online questionnaire piloted beforehand and reviewed by three social-science research professionals; fieldwork by Netquest (ISO 26362), single-invitation panel.
estimates.moderator_quote: Specifically, a survey was carried out in which a structured questionnaire was sent to the entire Spanish population aged between 18 and 25 years, with a sample of 5011 panel interviews being conducted online between 23 July and 14 August 2020.
estimates.notes: denom_scope=population per the standing rule that surveys are always population. platform_norm=survey because the item is explicitly medium-agnostic ('through any medium'), not restricted to social media. breadth coded 'false' rather than 'fabricated' because respondents were cued with the broad wording 'fake news, a rumor, a hoax, a lie', even though the paper's cited EJN definition is narrower (deliberately fabricated). Population is 18-25 year-olds only - a general-public age slice, not an elite or professional group. Lifetime ('at some time') window, so this is an upper-bound recall estimate. The moderator quote reads '5011' in the text file: that is '501' followed by the superscript footnote marker 1 ('One more interview in addition to the scheduled sample were carried out and were included'); the sample is 501, as every table's Total column shows.

estimates.platform: Any medium (survey question wording: 'through any medium')
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who say they have ever spread a fake news item through any medium knowing that it was fake
estimates.value_raw: Have spread fake news 6.6% (Table 14, Total n = 501); 33 individuals reported in Table 15 as 'Individuals Who Have Knowingly Spread Fake News'
estimates.denominator: 501 Spanish adults aged 18-25 interviewed online (Netquest panel, quota-matched to the National Institute of Statistics distribution)
estimates.definition: Respondent answered yes to Q10: 'Have you ever spread a fake news item through any medium knowing that it was fake?' - i.e. KNOWING dissemination only.
estimates.misinfo_def: "The Ethical Journalism Network (EJN) defines fake news as 'information deliberately fabricated and published with the intention to deceive and mislead others into believing falsehoods or doubting verifiable facts'"
estimates.source_quote: We found 87.6% of young people have at some time received fake news, especially women (91.5%), those with the highest level of education (93.7%) and social class (90.7%), while 6.6% claim to have spread fake news at some point, compared to 93.5% who do not tend to spread such news (Table 14).
estimates.page_loc: Section 3.3 Dissemination of Fake News, p. 11; Table 14, p. 12
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Pure respondent self-report; single dichotomous questionnaire item (Q10). No external verification. Socially sensitive item (admitting knowing dissemination), so under-reporting is likely.
estimates.moderator_quote: Q.10: Have you ever spread a fake news item through any medium knowing that it was fake?
estimates.notes: IMPORTANT for comparability: this is KNOWING sharing only ('knowing that it was fake'), a much stricter numerator than the usual 'have you ever shared something that turned out to be false' item, and 48.5% of these 33 self-reported spreaders say they always did it in order to WARN others that the item was fake news (Table 15). This is a distinct measure from the exposure row, hence a separate row rather than a definition_variant.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT EXTRACTED, deliberately: (1) 59.5% think they know how to identify fake news 'very well or quite well' (Table 9) - self-assessed discernment ability, not exposure or sharing, so excluded per the belief/discernment exclusion. (2) 39.5% always check whether news is true, 55.7% sometimes, 4.8% never (Table 11); 40.7% verify via fact-checking sites - verification behaviour, not a misinformation share. (3) 76.8% attach great importance to media literacy; 76.2% know of no literacy programme; 23.5% of the 119 who knew of a course took one - literacy/training measures, out of scope. (4) 82.0% say incongruity makes them think a news item is fake and 58.5% say 'if it comes from social networks like WhatsApp' (Table 10) - cues to suspicion, not exposure. (5) Table 15's within-spreader percentages (n = 33) are motive breakdowns of the 6.6%, not separate prevalence estimates. (6) Reported subgroup values for the two extracted rows (received: women 91.5%, third grade 93.7%, high social class 90.7%; spread: 18-19 yrs 8.6%) were not made into rows because they are demographic subgroups of the headline figure. (7) Minor numerical inconsistency in the source: the text says 'the results indicate that 59.5% of 10 young people think...' and Table 9's third-grade column reads '69.35'/'69.3'; neither affects the extracted rows. (8) The sample is 501 (one extra interview above the planned 500), which the paper flags in a footnote.

rob.design: Cross-sectional online panel survey; structured questionnaire piloted and pre-reviewed by three social-science research professionals; fieldwork by Netquest (ISO 26362 certified, single-invitation community, reducing self-selection and duplication); 501 interviews of Spanish 18-25 year-olds, 23 July - 14 August 2020, quotas on sex, age, region and social class matched to National Institute of Statistics proportions; stated sampling error +/-4.47% at 95% confidence; significance testing by t-test of proportions across segments. No response rate, no weighting details, no test-retest or validation of the self-report items; all misinformation measures are single-item self-reports.
rob.item6_quote: The Ethical Journalism Network (EJN) defines fake news as "information deliberately fabricated and published with the intention to deceive and mislead others into believing falsehoods or doubting verifiable facts" [17].
rob.item10_quote: We found 87.6% of young people have at some time received fake news, especially women (91.5%), those with the highest level of education (93.7%) and social class (90.7%), while 6.6% claim to have spread fake news at some point, compared to 93.5% who do not tend to spread such news (Table 14).
